decisions.title: Design regional recovery around the complete dependency graph
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Change and recoverySuggested owner Reliability architecture ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Managed inference availability does not automatically reproduce the application's identity, data, catalog, tools and spending authority in another Region. Cross-region inference and customer disaster recovery address different boundaries. Recovery objectives must cover the whole business path and its approved geography.

Options considered

  • Selected: explicit regional dependency inventories and recovery procedures with approved destinations.
  • Conditional: warm secondary application capacity where the recovery objective justifies its cost.
  • Rejected: equating an inference profile with automatic replication of all application state and controls.

Proposed decision

Define recovery time and data-loss objectives per workload, then choose single-region recovery or a qualified secondary deployment. Pre-provision permissions, model access, quotas, endpoints, keys and required data resources. Transfer spending authority safely during failover and preserve operation identities. Keep geography restrictions intact even when they require service degradation rather than unrestricted rerouting.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Recovery confidence requires rehearsal and secondary-resource cost.
  • Some stateful service resources need reconstruction or workflow-level recovery rather than a portable snapshot.

Required validation

  • A regional-loss exercise measures recovery of inference, authorization, retrieval, job tracking, tool execution and accounting as one path.
  • Simultaneous primary/secondary activity cannot exceed allocated spending authority or produce duplicate business effects.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when recovery objectives, data replication, profile destinations or regional feature availability changes, and after any failover exposes an unmodeled dependency.

Dependencies BR-ADR-004 · BR-ADR-008 · BR-ADR-017 · BR-ADR-019 · BR-ADR-023

decisions.title: Qualify SLOs with realistic workloads and client-observed timing
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Capacity and reliabilitySuggested owner Service reliability ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Published service capabilities and vendor performance descriptions do not establish the application's tail latency, completion rate or quality under its actual workload. Queueing, token length, tools, retrieval and policy processing contribute to user experience and may dominate the inference time.

Options considered

  • Selected: workload-specific SLO qualification with client timing and complete business outcomes.
  • Rejected: adopting generic throughput claims or tier descriptions as measured guarantees.
  • Conditional: different SLOs for interactive, batch, media and agent workflows with separate admission policies.

Proposed decision

Define success, denial, interruption and dependency failure precisely before testing. Measure first useful output, final completion, queue delay, token throughput, tool duration and cost at realistic concurrency and content sizes. Include cold paths and failures. Choose targets with application owners after evidence exists, then allocate error budgets to controllable customer dependencies and managed-service exposure.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Targets become defensible and useful for capacity decisions, but qualification requires representative traffic and evaluation data.
  • Separating legitimate policy denials from technical failures avoids misleading availability reports without hiding user impact.

Required validation

  • A reproducible test report states account quotas, endpoint, model, tier, SDK, token distribution and every enabled dependency.
  • Load and fault scenarios meet agreed completion, quality and cost criteria with confidence intervals or documented sample limitations.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when workload distributions, model versions, routing, service tiers or dependency topology change, and whenever incidents invalidate the original performance assumptions.

Dependencies BR-ADR-010 · BR-ADR-012 · BR-ADR-014 · BR-ADR-021

decisions.title: Inventory state and prove customer recovery and deletion
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Workflow stateSuggested owner Data platform ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Responses, files, sessions, job outputs, retrieval indexes and application records have different owners and lifetimes. A managed service resource identifier is not a backup strategy. Recovery and deletion decisions must be compatible with the selected retention policy and the organization's evidence obligations.

Options considered

  • Selected: a state inventory with explicit system of record, lifecycle and recovery method for each object class.
  • Rejected: assuming all managed state is exportable, globally replicated or recoverable after deletion.
  • Conditional: deliberate stateless operation where service-side persistence is unnecessary or incompatible with policy.

Proposed decision

Store durable business intent and customer-controlled artifacts in approved systems with tested backup procedures. Record which managed objects can be recreated, retrieved or deleted through documented APIs, and which require application-level reconstruction. Bind state access to tenant and project/workspace scope where applicable. Test retention enforcement and distinguish deletion of a logging configuration from deletion of already retained objects.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Recovery design may duplicate selected metadata while intentionally avoiding duplicate sensitive content.
  • Some managed state must be treated as disposable, making durable customer records essential for critical workflows.

Required validation

  • Restore exercises reconstruct a representative workflow and its authorization without relying on undocumented service snapshots.
  • Offboarding and retention tests demonstrate deletion or expiration across response state, logs, artifacts and customer stores, with approved audit exceptions recorded.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when stateful APIs, retention settings, export capabilities or recovery objectives change, and before storing a new class of sensitive information.

decisions.title: Preserve ingestion lineage and authorization metadata
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Retrieval and knowledgeSuggested owner Knowledge platform ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Retrieval quality and confidentiality depend on how source documents become chunks, embeddings and indexed permissions. The managed and customer-managed knowledge-base variants have different boundaries. An ingestion success status does not prove correct access metadata, freshness or reversible deletion of derived content.

Options considered

  • Selected: versioned ingestion configuration and source-to-index lineage with permission provenance.
  • Rejected: bulk ingestion without document ownership and authorization metadata.
  • Conditional: custom parsing or transformation only after deterministic behavior and isolation are qualified.

Proposed decision

Choose the knowledge-base variant deliberately and record source connectors, parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing and ACL behavior. Preserve document identifiers, source versions and effective access metadata through transformations. Separate ingestion roles from query roles. Define sync freshness, failed-document handling and deletion propagation objectives, and retain reproducible source manifests needed to rebuild an index safely.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Lineage improves explainability and recovery but increases metadata and synchronization work.
  • Changing chunking or embeddings becomes a data migration requiring retrieval and authorization requalification.

Required validation

  • A fixture corpus with changed permissions, deleted files, duplicate identifiers and malformed documents produces expected searchable results and exclusions.
  • An index rebuild from approved sources preserves provenance and access boundaries within the declared freshness objective.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when connectors, document permissions, parsers, embeddings or knowledge-base variant changes, and after any stale or unauthorized document is returned.

Dependencies BR-ADR-007 · BR-ADR-009 · BR-ADR-023 · BR-ADR-027

decisions.title: Authorize retrieval independently from generation
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Retrieval and knowledgeSuggested owner Application security ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

An index filter is not user authentication, and retrieved content remains untrusted input to the model. Shared vector stores or knowledge bases can create cross-tenant disclosure paths even when inference roles are correctly scoped. Authorization must be established before relevant content reaches generation.

Options considered

  • Selected: server-derived retrieval scope with negative tenant and document tests.
  • Conditional: shared stores only with qualified partitioning, filtering and administration boundaries.
  • Rejected: client-chosen ACL identities or unrestricted retrieval followed by attempted output redaction.

Proposed decision

Authenticate the user, derive permitted retrieval identity and filters from trusted policy, and apply the selected knowledge-base variant's documented controls. Treat document text and citations as untrusted data. Keep database credentials and query permissions narrowly scoped, and use separate stores where isolation cannot be demonstrated. Qualify retrieval-only and generation composition independently, including managed-variant API limitations.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Authorization remains understandable and testable at the content boundary.
  • Stronger store separation increases operating cost; filter-based sharing requires ongoing regression coverage and permission-freshness monitoring.

Required validation

  • Users cannot retrieve another tenant's documents through direct retrieval, generated answers, citations, reranking or alternate query APIs.
  • Revoked access and group changes meet the documented freshness bound, and prompt injection in retrieved content cannot grant new tool or data permissions.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when retrieval APIs, connectors, ACL semantics, shared-store topology or identity delegation changes, and after any disclosure or permission-freshness incident.

decisions.title: Separate legacy Agents Classic from new orchestration
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Agents and toolsSuggested owner Agent platform ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Agents Classic now has account-eligibility and maintenance constraints described in the architecture chapter. A greenfield reference design cannot assume new Classic creation is available. Existing deployments still need controlled tool execution and an evidence-based migration path that preserves business behavior.

Options considered

  • Selected: customer orchestration or separately qualified AgentCore capabilities for new agent designs.
  • Conditional: continued Classic operation only in eligible existing accounts with a documented lifecycle plan.
  • Rejected: making new Classic provisioning a universal onboarding prerequisite.

Proposed decision

For new workloads, select an orchestration implementation explicitly and give it no broader tool authority than the application requires. For eligible Classic deployments, inventory aliases, action groups, versions and dependencies before change. Prefer return-control or an equivalently controlled executor for sensitive actions, with independent authorization, schema validation, approval and idempotency outside model reasoning.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • New and existing agent estates may use different control planes during migration.
  • An orchestration choice does not delegate business authorization to the model or remove customer responsibility for tool side effects.

Required validation

  • A new-account onboarding test confirms the selected non-Classic path and all required service entitlements.
  • Tool fixtures reject unauthorized arguments, replayed actions and injected instructions; migration comparisons preserve approved business outcomes and audit correlation.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when Classic lifecycle guidance, account eligibility, AgentCore capabilities or application tool requirements change, and before extending a legacy orchestration dependency.

decisions.title: Bind sessions and memory to authenticated ownership
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Agents and toolsSuggested owner Conversation platform ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Conversation state can carry sensitive history and affect later actions. A session or memory identifier supplied by a client is only a reference, not proof of ownership. Legacy Classic memory and any newly selected orchestration memory must be evaluated under their own service contracts.

Options considered

  • Selected: server-issued session mappings bound to authenticated tenant and user context.
  • Conditional: persistent memory only for explicit product requirements with deletion and quality controls.
  • Rejected: globally reusable client-chosen identifiers or transferring unreviewed memory between users and orchestrators.

Proposed decision

Maintain an authorization mapping for every session and memory resource. Choose retention, sharing and deletion behavior deliberately, and minimize what becomes persistent memory. Reauthorize sensitive actions even when prior history suggests permission. For Classic, qualify its documented memory/session behavior in eligible accounts; for new orchestration, select and test the distinct state service instead of assuming compatibility.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Memory can improve continuity while increasing privacy, poisoning and stale-authorization risks.
  • Migration may require deliberate summarization or abandonment of old state rather than mechanical identifier reuse.

Required validation

  • Cross-user session and memory identifiers fail to disclose history or influence another user's workflow.
  • Deletion, expiry, concurrent turns, poisoned summaries and revoked permissions produce documented behavior without bypassing current authorization.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when memory providers, sharing features, retention requirements or orchestration platforms change, and after any history disclosure or action based on stale authority.

decisions.title: Promote immutable prompt and flow versions
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Application lifecycleSuggested owner Prompt and workflow ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Prompt text and flow structure are executable application behavior even when stored in a managed authoring service. A mutable draft can change model choices, tool access or business outcomes without an application deployment. Versioning therefore needs the same review discipline as code.

Options considered

  • Selected: immutable production prompt/flow versions with controlled aliases and release records.
  • Rejected: production invocation of continuously edited drafts.
  • Conditional: separate experimentation resources with restricted data and permissions, followed by explicit promotion.

Proposed decision

Store prompt templates, variable schemas, flow definitions and referenced resources under review. Create production versions only after contract, safety and quality checks, and bind aliases through the release manifest. Validate caller-supplied variables and keep tool credentials outside prompt content. Track dependencies on models, policies, retrieval and execution roles so a seemingly textual change receives appropriate review.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Managed authoring remains usable while changes become attributable and reproducible.
  • Version proliferation requires retention and cleanup policies that preserve necessary rollback and audit evidence.

Required validation

  • Production invocations resolve to approved versions, and unauthorized draft or alias changes are denied and audited.
  • A promoted version and its rollback reproduce expected variable validation, resource selection and workflow outcomes across representative cases.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when prompt tooling, flow capabilities, alias semantics or approval responsibilities change, and whenever an incident cannot be traced to an exact behavioral version.

decisions.title: Keep application and retrieval quality acceptance with the product owner
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Application lifecycleSuggested owner Application evaluation ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Successful API calls and safe-content filters do not establish that an answer is correct, useful or faithful to authorized evidence. Evaluation must represent the product's users and consequences. Managed evaluation facilities can assist measurement without deciding the organization's acceptable failure modes.

Options considered

  • Selected: versioned task-specific datasets and explicit product acceptance criteria.
  • Conditional: managed model/RAG evaluation for repeatable measurements with reviewed data and judge settings.
  • Rejected: one aggregate benchmark score as sufficient approval for all tenants and use cases.

Proposed decision

Define representative, difficult and adversarial cases with expected outcomes and cohort labels. Evaluate retrieval quality, grounded answers, tool correctness, refusals, latency and cost separately. Record evaluator configuration and use human review where automated judgments are unreliable. Gate changes to models, prompts, routing, indexes and guardrails, then compare production feedback with offline expectations.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Quality ownership stays close to business consequences, requiring ongoing dataset maintenance.
  • Automated judging improves scale but can introduce bias and should not silently replace domain review.

Required validation

  • A candidate release passes agreed thresholds across critical cohorts rather than only an overall average.
  • Evaluation records reproduce the selected model, prompt, retrieval corpus, policy and judge versions without exposing unauthorized test data.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when user tasks, risk tolerance, source content or failure distributions change, and when production errors reveal blind spots in the evaluation set.

decisions.title: Qualify customization and imported models as separate products
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Application lifecycleSuggested owner Model engineering ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Customization and model import introduce training data, artifacts, serving options and lifecycle dependencies beyond ordinary foundation-model invocation. Familiar API shapes do not prove equal support for guardrails, capacity, streaming or recovery. Their value must be measured against a simpler prompting or retrieval baseline.

Options considered

  • Selected: separate qualification records for each customized or imported model artifact.
  • Rejected: automatic production trust because a job completed or an import was accepted.
  • Conditional: customization only after a demonstrated quality, latency or economics benefit over simpler alternatives.

Proposed decision

Record data rights, provenance, training configuration, artifact checksums where customer-accessible, evaluation results and supported serving contract. Isolate training and import roles from production invocation. Assess model-specific capacity, warm-up, retention and recovery requirements, including base-model lifecycle exposure. Promote through the same catalog and quality gates as other models, retaining a tested alternative where the custom path is unavailable.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Specialized models can improve a task while increasing data governance and deployment complexity.
  • Import portability remains bounded by supported formats and licenses; it is not a blanket promise of cross-service equivalence.

Required validation

  • Reproducibility checks identify the source data, artifact and training/import configuration for every production deployment.
  • The deployed artifact meets approved quality, capacity, policy and recovery tests, including denied artifact access and unavailable serving capacity.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when training data, base model, import support, license or serving mode changes, and when maintenance cost exceeds the demonstrated product benefit.

Dependencies BR-ADR-003 · BR-ADR-009 · BR-ADR-010 · BR-ADR-024 · BR-ADR-033

decisions.title: Review model entitlements and capacity commitments explicitly
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Commercial and lifecycleSuggested owner Platform procurement ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Availability in a service catalog does not settle account entitlement, model terms, Marketplace deployment requirements or capacity economics. Different purchase and serving paths can create recurring charges and permissions beyond a simple token invoice. Operational approval needs an identifiable commercial owner.

Options considered

  • Selected: a model-by-model entitlement and commercial review tied to the catalog.
  • Rejected: treating all Bedrock models and tiers as interchangeable purchases.
  • Conditional: Marketplace endpoints or capacity commitments only after workload qualification and exit-cost review.

Proposed decision

Document access prerequisites, applicable provider terms, permitted data classes, endpoint support and charging basis for each production option. Approve reservation duration, overflow, minimum allocation and cancellation ownership before commitment. Separate experiment subscriptions from production. Confirm that required models and tiers are available in the target account and Regions, with support escalation and termination procedures recorded.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Procurement becomes part of release readiness, preventing hidden commitments and inaccessible dependencies.
  • Some technically attractive capabilities may remain unapproved because their terms, capacity or exit cost do not fit the workload.

Required validation

  • A target-account qualification demonstrates entitlement, actual serving tier and attribution before production traffic is admitted.
  • A financial review explains steady-state, peak, idle and termination cost, including every separately billed dependent service.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when provider terms, model access, Marketplace packaging, service tiers or expected utilization change, and before renewing any capacity commitment.

Dependencies BR-ADR-003 · BR-ADR-010 · BR-ADR-018 · BR-ADR-034

decisions.title: Treat AgentCore as a separately selected service architecture
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Agents and toolsSuggested owner Agent infrastructure ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

AgentCore offers capabilities beyond Bedrock inference, but selecting Bedrock does not automatically select an agent runtime, gateway, identity service, memory store or evaluation stack. Those components have distinct permissions, state and operational responsibilities that need individual design and entitlement review.

Options considered

  • Selected: explicit selection and qualification of each required AgentCore capability.
  • Rejected: depicting AgentCore as an implicit internal component of the inference gateway.
  • Conditional: customer-operated alternatives where portability, control or existing infrastructure better satisfies requirements.

Proposed decision

Create a separate component inventory for selected AgentCore services, including authentication, resource scope, tools, memory, network access, regional processing and pricing. Integrate them through the application contract and shared audit identifiers without merging trust boundaries. Require independent authorization for external tools and isolate execution from model text. Keep unused capabilities disabled or unprovisioned.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Agent infrastructure can be adopted incrementally while preserving clear ownership.
  • Multiple managed services still require integration, operational qualification and a coherent end-to-end incident process.

Required validation

  • An architecture review assigns roles, state, network paths and recovery responsibilities to each selected component.
  • Tool discovery, execution, identity exchange and memory access tests reject unauthorized callers and cross-tenant resource references.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when additional AgentCore services become necessary, processing locations change, or integration cost and portability requirements favor a different orchestration boundary.

Dependencies BR-ADR-001 · BR-ADR-006 · BR-ADR-008 · BR-ADR-009 · BR-ADR-030 · BR-ADR-031

decisions.title: Pin customer artifacts and test SDK behavior changes
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Change and recoverySuggested owner Software supply-chain ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Managed inference removes customer patching of the provider's internal serving fleet, but applications still ship SDKs, compatibility adapters, infrastructure providers, tool executors and possibly a gateway. Those artifacts can alter security and retry behavior independently of the selected model catalog.

Options considered

  • Selected: immutable customer release artifacts with dependency provenance and controlled updates.
  • Rejected: mutable image tags or uncontrolled runtime downloads in privileged production components.
  • Conditional: expedited patching based on exposure, followed by complete regression evidence.

Proposed decision

Inventory and pin customer-controlled dependencies, build artifacts and deployment providers. Scan and review their provenance through the organization's normal supply-chain process. Test SDK changes against authentication, retries, streaming, metadata and error fixtures before promotion. Maintain emergency revocation and redeployment procedures for compromised credentials or artifacts, and distinguish customer updates from service changes communicated by AWS.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The smaller customer infrastructure footprint still requires disciplined patching and artifact custody.
  • Reproducibility enables incident attribution but must not become an excuse to remain on unsupported dependencies.

Required validation

  • A clean build reconstructs the approved artifact and dependency inventory with verifiable origin.
  • A dependency update passes the bounded contract suite and shows no unexpected retry amplification, telemetry leakage or permission expansion.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when SDK support, vulnerability exposure, build systems or third-party adapters change, and after any unexplained difference between supposedly identical deployments.

decisions.title: Operate a model-access and deprecation calendar
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Commercial and lifecycleSuggested owner Model portfolio ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Model lifecycle rules vary by launch cohort and model card, and access can depend on account eligibility and continued usage. Applications therefore need a migration plan before a retirement announcement becomes urgent. An alias alone cannot preserve a model that the service stops offering.

Options considered

  • Selected: a reviewed lifecycle calendar with successor evaluation and accountable migration dates.
  • Rejected: waiting for failed production requests to reveal access or retirement changes.
  • Conditional: extended or private access only as a temporary documented commercial exception.

Proposed decision

Record current lifecycle evidence, access prerequisites and latest safe migration dates for every catalog entry. Monitor AWS notices and model cards, then qualify successors through task-specific evaluations. Include custom deployments and legacy orchestration dependencies in impact analysis. Test access in recovery accounts rather than assuming production entitlement transfers, and remove retired choices from new-workload onboarding.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Planned migrations reduce emergency changes but require continuous portfolio attention.
  • Successor models may change quality, pricing, retention and API support, making replacement a product decision.

Required validation

  • Every production model has an owner, lifecycle evidence and a tested or scheduled successor strategy.
  • A simulated access loss or retirement routes work only to an approved alternative and produces clear operational and user-facing outcomes.

Revisit trigger

Revisit on lifecycle announcements, account-access changes, model-card revisions or a failed successor evaluation, and before relying on a model for a new long-lived product.

Dependencies BR-ADR-003 · BR-ADR-024 · BR-ADR-033 · BR-ADR-035

decisions.title: Make shared responsibility operational through runbooks
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations governanceSuggested owner Service operations ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

A managed service incident and a customer policy, identity or workflow incident can look similar to the caller. Reliable response requires evidence and ownership across that boundary. Support entitlements and escalation procedures need to match the business objective rather than remain procurement assumptions.

Options considered

  • Selected: runbooks assigning customer action, AWS escalation and business communication responsibilities.
  • Rejected: routing every failure to AWS or expecting cloud support to repair application authorization and data.
  • Conditional: higher support commitments where response requirements and service criticality justify them.

Proposed decision

Define incident classes for throttling, model errors, credential exposure, policy bypass, content leakage, job ambiguity, retrieval staleness and regional loss. Give operators bounded containment actions and protected evidence access. Record support contacts and contractual scope, including separately selected services. Rehearse recovery and customer communication with application owners, and track corrective actions to configuration or ADR revisions.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Clear ownership shortens diagnosis while exposing dependencies the organization must staff.
  • Runbooks cannot guarantee provider recovery time; business degradation choices remain necessary.

Required validation

  • A tabletop incident identifies the responsible role, safe containment action, required evidence and escalation route without administrative improvisation.
  • A technical exercise demonstrates credential containment, preserved audit evidence and recovery of a representative critical workflow.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when support contracts, service criticality, team ownership or dependency boundaries change, and after every material incident or failed exercise.

decisions.title: Maintain an exit path and an evidence-based decision lifecycle
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Commercial and lifecycleSuggested owner Architecture governance ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

The proposed decisions describe a reference architecture, not accepted organizational policy or AWS historical reasoning. Their usefulness depends on owners replacing assumptions with evidence and revisiting tradeoffs. An exit strategy must account for managed state and behavior, not only compatible inference syntax.

Options considered

  • Selected: time-bounded decision review and a tested minimal portability path.
  • Rejected: claiming universal portability from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint or permanently accepting this report unchanged.
  • Conditional: deeper managed features where their product value exceeds documented migration and recovery costs.

Proposed decision

Keep every record Proposed until accountable owners review scope, evidence, costs and acceptance results. Record acceptance, supersession or rejection without erasing rationale. Maintain exportable customer data, prompt and policy definitions, evaluation cases and logical model contracts where feasible. Rehearse one alternate inference path and document irreducible dependencies on managed retrieval, state, tools and customized artifacts.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The organization gains an explicit lock-in budget and actionable review process.
  • Full feature parity may be impractical; exit plans can choose reduced functionality with clearly accepted business consequences.

Required validation

  • A decision review produces named owners, dated evidence and unresolved conditions without marking unexecuted gates as passed.
  • An exit exercise moves a representative workload and authorized data to the chosen alternative, measuring lost features, quality, effort and operational cost.

Revisit trigger

Revisit at agreed portfolio intervals and when commercial terms, service lifecycle, compliance obligations or migration economics materially change the original adoption case.

decisions.title: Operate a shared enterprise gateway service
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Service contractSuggested owner Platform architecture leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Several applications may need model access while identity, provider contracts and cost policy remain organization-wide concerns. Distributing these responsibilities across every application increases variation. A shared gateway introduces a dependency that requires an explicit operating owner and a bounded service contract.

Options considered

  • SDK in every application: simplest local integration, but each team owns credentials, governance and upgrades independently.
  • Shared gateway: selected for consistent controls and attribution, accepting an additional service and network dependency.
  • Gateway plus unrestricted direct access: rejected for production because policy coverage would depend on individual client behavior.

Proposed decision

Offer production model access through an organization-owned gateway endpoint. Applications retain business authorization, workflow orchestration and result validation. SDK use remains optional behind the gateway contract. Establish a service owner, incident route and onboarding policy before accepting production traffic, with direct provider access restricted to separately approved exceptions.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Central ownership can make model access and spend policy easier to change, while platform availability becomes part of every participating application's dependency model.
  • Provider credentials concentrate in a smaller operational boundary; that boundary needs stronger access management, maintenance discipline and a documented exception process.

Required validation

  • A representative application authenticates with its own workload identity, calls an approved alias and emits a trace attributable to its team.
  • An application lacking an approved exception cannot reach providers directly; disabling its gateway identity blocks further paid upstream calls.

Revisit trigger

Reassess when the application portfolio, operating capacity or existing enterprise API platform changes enough to alter the value of central ownership.

Dependencies None; foundational decision.

decisions.title: Qualify the stable Python-hosted gateway and native paths separately
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Service contractSuggested owner Gateway engineering leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A gateway's host runtime and native components are different architectural choices. The baseline must identify both, including components used automatically by its pinned artifact. Optional per-model execution paths and a standalone server require distinct compatibility, control and recovery evidence.

Options considered

  • Stable Python-hosted gateway: selected as the baseline, including the native components that the chosen artifact loads automatically.
  • Optional per-model Rust paths: keep off initially, then qualify their behavior and recovery separately against the baseline.
  • Standalone Axum gateway: evaluate as a distinct deployment; do not equate it with native modules inside the hosted gateway.

Proposed decision

Pin the supported stable Python-hosted gateway for baseline qualification and inventory every native component used automatically by that artifact. Disable optional per-model Rust paths during this baseline. Qualify those optional paths separately from the standalone Axum gateway using the same control corpus. Do not assume every native component has a Python fallback or opt-out.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The Python-hosted baseline includes automatically loaded native dependencies, which belong in provenance, compatibility and operational review alongside the host application.
  • Separate qualification clarifies which behavior changes with an optional path or a different server, while some built-in native components may offer no Python replacement.

Required validation

  • The baseline artifact has a reviewed native-component inventory and passes the endpoint/control matrix with optional per-model Rust paths disabled.
  • Each optional path and standalone Axum candidate independently demonstrates expected stream, error, policy and accounting outcomes and its documented recovery mechanism.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when native-component maturity, application requirements or measured gateway resource costs create a concrete reason to change the qualified production execution path.

Dependencies ADR-001

decisions.title: Publish a bounded endpoint and capability contract
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Service contractSuggested owner API platform product ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

A broad upstream endpoint catalog does not establish identical behavior across providers, transports or client SDKs. Applications need predictable guarantees for the operations they actually use. Exposing every available route immediately also enlarges policy coverage and support obligations without a demonstrated business requirement.

Options considered

  • Expose all upstream routes: rejected because support and control coverage would expand faster than application validation.
  • Approve endpoint-provider combinations: selected to make compatibility, security and operational guarantees explicit and testable.
  • Force one generic text API: rejected where necessary streaming, structured output or stateful capabilities cannot be expressed faithfully.

Proposed decision

Maintain an approved matrix of endpoint, provider, model family, client version and required capabilities. Initially expose only combinations with a named application owner and acceptance evidence. Document unsupported parameters, translation differences, streaming events and error semantics. Expand the contract through versioned review rather than treating upstream additions as automatic availability.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Applications gain a dependable support boundary, while onboarding unusual capabilities may require platform engineering and additional validation time.
  • An endpoint advertised by LiteLLM can remain unavailable internally until identity, data policy, observability and operational behavior are qualified for that combination.

Required validation

  • Contract tests exercise each supported combination with ordinary requests, malformed inputs, policy rejection and representative provider failures.
  • The ingress and gateway deny unapproved endpoint families; documentation identifies the exact capability and client versions the organization commits to support.

Revisit trigger

Review when an application requires an excluded capability, a provider changes its contract or an upgrade changes previously accepted behavior.

Dependencies ADR-001 · ADR-002

decisions.title: Version logical model aliases and their service promises
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Service contractSuggested owner Model platform leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Applications benefit from an organization-owned model name, but an alias can hide changes in quality, context size, output format, data location or cost. A silent remapping can therefore break application assumptions even when the HTTP interface and response schema remain unchanged.

Options considered

  • Provider model names in application code: transparent but tightly couples application releases to provider naming and deployment choices.
  • Versioned logical aliases: selected to separate application intent from approved implementations while retaining explicit behavioral promises.
  • Unversioned automatic remapping: rejected for material behavior changes because applications would inherit unreviewed quality and policy differences.

Proposed decision

Define aliases by supported task and capability class, with documented provider set, context limits, response requirements, data policy and cost envelope. Version aliases for material behavior changes. Permit deployment substitutions only inside the published promise and after application evaluations pass; record the actual resolved deployment in operational metadata.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Applications can change infrastructure independently from their user-facing behavior, but the platform must manage alias lifecycle, deprecation and communication deliberately.
  • Some provider innovations require a new alias or application approval instead of an immediate global remapping, creating a useful but real adoption delay.

Required validation

  • Every alias resolves only to its approved deployment set, and request telemetry identifies the implementation selected for each attempt.
  • A proposed remapping passes the consuming applications' evaluation corpus and capability checks before its traffic allocation increases.

Revisit trigger

Reassess an alias when its provider retires a model, its task promise changes or maintenance cost exceeds the value of preserving compatibility.

Dependencies ADR-003

decisions.title: Issue distinct workload keys with accountable ownership
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and trustSuggested owner Identity and access management leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Production applications, individual developers and administrative automation have different lifecycles. Sharing one credential across them obscures attribution and makes revocation disruptive. Linking a durable production dependency to an employee's personal access can also create an avoidable outage during routine personnel changes.

Options considered

  • One shared master credential: rejected because compromise or rotation affects every application and grants excessive administrative authority.
  • Human-owned application keys: convenient initially, but rejected for durable services whose lifecycle exceeds a person's membership.
  • Scoped workload service accounts: selected for independent ownership, environment separation, model access and revocation without unrelated application disruption.

Proposed decision

Create one service account identity per production workload, environment and materially different privilege set. Associate it with a responsible team and bounded model access. Use separate human identities for development and administration. Prefer short-lived credentials where client support is proven, and inventory rotation, expiry and recovery ownership for remaining virtual keys.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Credential inventory grows, but incidents and application retirement can be handled without rotating every consumer or guessing which workload caused usage.
  • Service-account continuity must be balanced with ownership review so keys that survive staff departures do not become forgotten, indefinitely authorized assets.

Required validation

  • Revoking one workload identity stops its requests on every replica without interrupting another application's approved traffic.
  • Removing a human owner has the documented effect on personal keys while the team service account continues under a verified remaining owner.

Revisit trigger

Review when workload identity support improves, organizational ownership changes or a credential incident exposes a weakness in key scope or lifecycle.

Dependencies ADR-001

decisions.title: Validate JWT issuer, audience and entitlement claims explicitly
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and trustSuggested owner Identity security architectDate 6 October 2026

Context

A token can have a valid signature while targeting another application or carrying claims with different meanings. Multiple identity providers make these ambiguities more likely. Authentication must establish both who issued the token and why the gateway should accept its intended audience and permissions.

Options considered

  • Global JWKS configuration alone: rejected because cryptographic verification does not express the complete issuer, audience and entitlement boundary.
  • Explicit issuer-specific trust configuration: selected to bind signing keys and claim mappings to each approved identity provider.
  • Custom authentication code: reserve for unmet requirements because it adds privileged logic and a separate security maintenance obligation.

Proposed decision

Configure exact expected issuer and audience values, stable identity claims and explicit entitlement mappings. For an issuer allowlist, remove unintended global fallback paths. Define the permitted lifetime of cached signing keys during IdP outages. Treat caller-supplied metadata as descriptive unless it is independently authenticated and authorized for the asserted purpose.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Tokens for other applications are rejected even when the identity provider shares signing keys, reducing accidental trust across organizational services.
  • Identity-provider onboarding and key rotation require controlled tests; strict trust policy may trade some outage tolerance for clearer revocation and authentication boundaries.

Required validation

  • Reject wrong-audience, unknown-issuer, expired and insufficiently scoped tokens, including a correctly signed token issued for another application.
  • Rotate signing keys and interrupt JWKS retrieval; observed acceptance and rejection remain within the agreed cache lifetime and recovery policy.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when adding an identity provider, changing claim semantics or accepting a different availability-versus-revocation tradeoff for signing-key outages in production.

decisions.title: Make tenant and resource isolation an explicit invariant
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and trustSuggested owner Platform security architectDate 6 October 2026

Context

Keys, teams and organizations organize access, but applications may also exchange file IDs, sessions, cached outputs and tool resources. These objects can outlive an individual request. Isolation must cover every lookup and mutation, not merely the permission to invoke a model endpoint.

Options considered

  • Model-level access only: rejected because access to a model does not authorize another tenant's stored resources or administrative data.
  • Application-only isolation: insufficient as the sole control when shared gateway endpoints directly expose resources and management operations.
  • Gateway plus application resource checks: selected, with independent deployments where the required boundary exceeds logical tenancy.

Proposed decision

Derive the tenant context from validated identity and enforce it for keys, budgets, logs, files, sessions, caches and tools. Document inheritance and empty-list semantics before provisioning. Require resource ownership on reads, polling, deletion and reuse of identifiers. Separate deployments and credentials where contractual or risk requirements demand stronger isolation.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Isolation becomes a measurable contract across resource lifecycles, increasing the test surface and the care needed when introducing new endpoint families.
  • A shared process and database remain a common security boundary even with correct logical permissions; stronger isolation can require additional infrastructure and license cost.

Required validation

  • Two tenants using identical prompts or exchanged resource identifiers cannot retrieve, modify or charge against each other's protected data and allocations.
  • Repeat isolation checks after key revocation, membership changes, cached authorization, replica lag and restoration of older state.

Revisit trigger

Review when onboarding a materially different trust domain, exposing a new stateful resource or changing organization/team inheritance and delegation within the service.

Dependencies ADR-005 · ADR-006

decisions.title: Restrict administrative access independently of inference traffic
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and trustSuggested owner Platform security operations leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A shared gateway serves both routine application requests and privileged changes to credentials, models and policy. Those traffic classes have different audiences and consequences. Treating the administrative UI and management APIs as ordinary public inference routes unnecessarily widens exposure and complicates individual accountability.

Options considered

  • Public combined routes with a shared password: rejected because a broadly reachable credential controls the entire service.
  • Private named administration: selected using network restrictions, identity-provider controls and minimal assigned administrative roles.
  • Network restriction without application authorization: rejected because an internal network is not proof of a caller's administrative entitlement.

Proposed decision

Expose management routes only through an approved administrative access path. Use named identities and IdP MFA, restrict proxy-admin membership and disable bootstrap environment login after recovery access is verified. Configure trusted proxy ranges for forwarded client identity. Keep application keys unable to mutate global credentials, routes or access policy.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Administrative activity becomes more attributable and less reachable, while emergency access must be maintained separately from ordinary user onboarding.
  • Route separation requires inventory and review when releases add management endpoints; UI failure and administrative lockout need procedures that do not weaken workload authentication.

Required validation

  • Workload keys and callers outside the administrative path cannot invoke privileged operations, including direct requests that bypass the UI.
  • Named administrators can recover access after bootstrap login is disabled; forged forwarding headers cannot change the effective trusted source identity.

Revisit trigger

Reassess when administrative automation, remote support or newly exposed endpoint families require a different access path or delegated privilege set.

Dependencies ADR-006 · ADR-007

decisions.title: Separate encryption material from rotating access credentials
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and trustSuggested owner Secrets management leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Access credentials should rotate routinely, while persisted encrypted values must remain readable throughout upgrades and recovery. Combining those purposes makes a simple credential replacement capable of disrupting stored provider configuration. The reference design needs separate ownership, backup and incident procedures for each secret category.

Options considered

  • Master key as both access and encryption material: rejected for new deployments because routine rotation becomes a data migration.
  • Dedicated stable salt plus rotating access secrets: selected, with restricted recovery handling and documented limitations on salt replacement.
  • External secret retrieval: use where useful, but evaluate integration entitlement and runtime availability rather than assuming it removes all local secret exposure.

Proposed decision

Set a dedicated strong salt before registering stored credentials and protect it independently from the master key. Rotate access credentials through their documented lifecycle. With a dedicated salt, change the master secret and restart replicas rather than using master-key re-encryption. Preserve an authorized recovery copy of encryption material alongside database recovery procedures.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Routine access-key rotation becomes simpler, but losing the stable encryption secret can make restored provider and tool credentials unusable.

  • Restore a database and its authorized salt into isolation, then prove stored model and tool credentials decrypt without exposing plaintext in logs.
  • Rotate master and provider credentials across replicas; old access fails while approved workloads continue after the documented rollout and recovery sequence.

Reopen for encryption-material disclosure, a mandatory rotation requirement or a vendor release that introduces a supported and recoverable in-place salt migration.

decisions.title: Bind egress and residency policy to approved routes
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and trustSuggested owner Cloud network and data governance leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Self-hosting places the gateway under organizational control, but requests may still leave through providers, guardrails, logging services and tools. A fallback or client-selected URL can alter the destination. Data locality must therefore be a property of every allowed route and auxiliary integration.

Options considered

  • Unrestricted outbound internet access: rejected because request extensions or configuration mistakes could bypass destination and residency review.
  • Approved destination policy: selected for providers and auxiliary services, with documented private endpoints and controlled onboarding.
  • A gateway-only residency label: rejected because it says nothing about where model processing, logging or tool execution occurs.

Proposed decision

Define approved destination, credential and data-location sets for each model alias and integration. Restrict request-supplied routing overrides and enforce egress controls where practical, including redirects and private-address handling. Require fallbacks, mirrors, logs and guardrail services to satisfy the same data policy as the original route before they can receive content.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Policy remains meaningful during failures and debugging, but adding providers or changing endpoint hostnames may require coordinated network and governance work.
  • Egress restrictions can break discovery, token refresh or observability unexpectedly unless those dependencies are inventoried and tested alongside inference destinations.

Required validation

  • Synthetic credentials and sensitive markers never reach unapproved hosts through alternate routing fields, redirects, error handling or optional callback paths.
  • Provider failover and auxiliary-service failures preserve the declared regional policy, with observable rejection when no compliant destination remains.

Revisit trigger

Review when provider contracts, approved regions, network architecture or auxiliary integrations change the set of permitted data recipients and processing locations.

decisions.title: Start with weighted routing among approved equivalent deployments
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner Gateway reliability leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Routing can optimize capacity, latency or cost, but extra logic introduces state and may change application behavior. Without a demonstrated need for adaptive selection, an understandable baseline helps attribute measured improvements or regressions to the routing strategy itself.

Options considered

  • Weighted selection within an approved alias: selected for a simple baseline that reflects known capacity and deployment eligibility.
  • Latency-, usage- or cost-adaptive routing: defer until representative measurements establish a benefit and state overhead is understood.
  • Unconstrained cheapest-model routing: rejected because lower price does not establish equivalent quality, capability, availability or data policy.

Proposed decision

Begin with simple-shuffle weighted selection across deployments that satisfy the same alias contract. Set weights from approved capacity allocations and validate them under realistic traffic. Keep cooldown and fallback eligibility explicit. Introduce adaptive or custom routing only through a measured experiment that preserves the alias's capability, cost and residency boundaries.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The baseline is easier to reason about during incidents and provides a comparison point, but it may not achieve the lowest possible latency or cost.
  • Uneven workloads and provider throttling still require capacity planning; weights should not be mistaken for guaranteed throughput or strict provider quota enforcement.

Required validation

  • Sustained representative traffic produces the intended approximate distribution while every chosen deployment remains inside the approved alias and residency set.
  • A throttled or failed deployment leaves rotation as intended, recovers without oscillation and does not trigger an unapproved fallback.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when measured tail latency, utilization or cost shows a material problem that an evaluated alternative routing strategy can address.

decisions.title: Assign one retry owner and an end-to-end deadline
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner Application reliability architectDate 6 October 2026

Context

Clients and gateways can independently retry requests, multiplying attempts, spending and latency. A timeout does not prove that upstream work never started. Retry policy must therefore reflect operation side effects, safe repetition and the client's total response deadline.

Options considered

  • Independent retries at every layer: rejected because attempt multiplication and cumulative deadlines become difficult to predict or explain.
  • Gateway-owned bounded retries: selected for approved transient failures, with clients following the published application-level recovery contract.
  • No retries anywhere: retain for unsafe operations, but reject as a universal policy where limited retry can recover transient failures.

Proposed decision

Make the gateway the primary retry owner for ordinary eligible inference calls. Publish one end-to-end deadline, a maximum attempt budget and retryable error classes. Disable redundant client retries where practical. Treat stateful submission, tool execution and already-committed streams separately, requiring evidence of safe repetition or explicit application recovery before another attempt.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Requests have a bounded latency and amplification envelope, but some transient failures will surface earlier than they would under unbounded layered retries.
  • Application teams must distinguish safe retry from duplicate side effects and may need idempotency or reconciliation beyond what a model gateway can provide.

Required validation

  • Inject provider throttling, connection failure and delayed responses; recorded upstream attempts and total latency stay within the declared request budget.
  • After partial stream delivery or an acknowledged side effect, retry behavior matches the endpoint contract and does not silently duplicate work.

Revisit trigger

Review when a provider changes failure semantics, client defaults change or a new operation introduces a different idempotency and deadline requirement.

decisions.title: Specify streaming, disconnect and cancellation behavior
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner Streaming API engineering leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Streaming changes when output becomes visible and how later failures can be reported. Long-lived requests retain resources and may continue consuming provider capacity after disconnect. Applications need explicit partial-output, timeout, usage and cancellation semantics for each approved transport.

Options considered

  • Transparent byte forwarding only: insufficient because clients also require error, accounting, cancellation and policy behavior across stream lifecycles.
  • Qualified streaming contract: selected with bounded connections, documented event shapes, disconnect handling and endpoint-specific completion accounting.
  • Buffer every response universally: reject where unnecessary because it removes streaming benefits and can create avoidable memory and latency costs.

Proposed decision

Define time to first output, idle timeout, total deadline, partial-error signaling and client-disconnect behavior for each streaming route. Propagate cancellation where supported and measure remaining upstream work. Preserve final usage when available without inventing missing usage. Enable full buffering only where required output policy justifies the latency and resource tradeoff.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Clients can handle incomplete responses deliberately, but some upstream protocols will provide weaker cancellation or usage evidence than others.
  • Long streams require concurrency and connection planning; cancellation success cannot be inferred solely from closing the client socket or returning a gateway error.

Required validation

  • Disconnect clients before output and midway through long streams; observe provider activity, resource release and accounting within an agreed operational bound.
  • Inject malformed events, idle stalls and mid-stream failures; clients receive the documented terminal outcome without duplicated or silently corrupted output.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when adding realtime or another streaming protocol, changing ingress limits or learning that cancellation and final-usage behavior differ by provider.

decisions.title: Make required guardrails preventive and route-specific
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner AI security policy leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Content controls can run before dispatch, concurrently or after output, providing different guarantees once streamed bytes or tool side effects are visible. The organization must distinguish mandatory prevention from monitoring and verify the endpoint and payload shapes actually covered.

Options considered

  • Client-selected guardrails: reject for mandatory policy because callers can omit them or choose weaker request settings.
  • Explicit always-on preventive controls: selected for required input and output policy, accepting documented latency and availability costs.
  • Audit-only scanning: retain for monitoring and evaluation, but do not describe it as preventing content that was already delivered.

Proposed decision

Attach mandatory guards through controlled server policy. Run required input checks before provider dispatch and explicitly configure output buffering when content must be blocked before delivery. Define fail behavior for unavailable or unsupported guards. Qualify each endpoint, provider, stream and payload shape, including cache hits and tool results, before asserting preventive coverage.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Required policy can add latency and reject traffic during guardrail outages; the business owner must accept that behavior rather than assuming scanning is free.
  • Guardrails reduce specific exposure but do not replace resource authorization, application quality evaluation or safe handling of generated code, queries and tool arguments.

Required validation

  • A prohibited synthetic marker never reaches the provider or client on preventive paths, including markers split across stream chunks and cached responses.
  • Missing registration, timeout, unsupported payload and guardrail-service failure produce the chosen observable denial or explicitly approved monitoring-only outcome.

Revisit trigger

Review after provider or guardrail upgrades, changes in policy, unacceptable false-positive rates or introduction of an endpoint outside the qualified coverage matrix.

decisions.title: Keep exact response caching off by default and tenant-partitioned
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner Data platform security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Response caching retains content and may reuse answers under a different identity or policy context. TTL and encryption address different risks from authorization. The reference gateway should not persist payloads merely because a coordination or cache backend is available.

Options considered

  • Cache every supported call automatically: rejected until privacy, authorization, freshness and invalidation requirements are established for those workloads.
  • Explicitly approved exact caching: selected with server-derived partitioning, retention and a tested relationship to access and guardrail checks.
  • Provider prompt caching only: consider separately because it has different semantics, storage responsibility and contractual behavior from gateway response reuse.

Proposed decision

Set exact response caching to off by default. Enable it only for approved workloads with a documented data class, TTL and invalidation strategy. Derive partitioning from trusted tenant and policy context rather than accepting a client namespace as authority. Exclude side-effecting, resource-sensitive or freshness-critical requests unless their complete identity and state semantics are proven.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Initial costs may be higher, but content retention and cross-context reuse are restricted until the workload demonstrates a worthwhile and safe benefit.
  • Cache-hit responses still require the declared access and content controls; model, prompt, retrieval-data or policy changes can require invalidation beyond ordinary time expiry.

Required validation

  • Identical prompts from different tenants and privilege contexts cannot retrieve another context's cached output, including after policy or membership changes.
  • No-store and configured retention behave as documented, and cache-hit requests still execute every control required by their approved policy.

Revisit trigger

Reopen for a workload with measured repetition, acceptable freshness requirements and enough expected cost or latency savings to justify cache qualification.

decisions.title: Evaluate semantic caching as a separate product decision
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner Application evaluation leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Semantically similar requests can require different answers because dates, negation, quantities or permissions differ. Semantic caching therefore changes application behavior and needs workload-specific evidence beyond exact-match correctness. A universal similarity threshold cannot establish the acceptable substitution risk.

Options considered

  • Enable semantic caching with a generic similarity threshold: rejected because similarity alone is not a workload-specific correctness guarantee.
  • Workload-specific semantic experiment: selected only after exact-cache isolation and a labeled acceptance corpus exist.
  • No semantic caching: retain as the production default when correctness, privacy or freshness costs outweigh demonstrated savings.

Proposed decision

Keep semantic caching disabled in the reference rollout. For a candidate workload, define labeled equivalent and nonequivalent request pairs, tenant boundaries, freshness windows and tolerated error rates. Evaluate the embedding model, threshold and invalidation together. Approve only a bounded use case whose measured savings exceed the accepted quality and operational costs.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The organization avoids silently changing answer semantics, while workloads with repetitive natural-language intent may initially miss a useful optimization.
  • Evaluation and monitoring become continuous responsibilities because changes to prompts, embeddings, corpus content and user behavior can invalidate an earlier similarity threshold.

Required validation

  • The labeled corpus covers negation, numerical changes, dates, identity and near-duplicate requests, with harmful cache substitutions below the approved threshold.
  • A controlled rollout measures actual savings, wrong-hit rate and freshness failures; disabling semantic reuse restores the baseline without deleting required durable state.

Revisit trigger

Review when exact caching leaves a material measured opportunity or when the workload, embedding model and acceptable substitution risk change substantially.

decisions.title: Use PostgreSQL as durable governance authority
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area State and governanceSuggested owner Database platform leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Governance needs durable identity, configuration and spending records across restarts and replicas. Ephemeral state can accelerate admission but cannot replace a recoverable record. Database absence and degradation therefore require deliberate operating policies, capacity planning and observable recovery behavior.

Options considered

  • DB-less proxy: rejected for the governed production service because durable keys, configuration and budget authority are required.
  • Managed PostgreSQL: selected for durable control records, backup, access restrictions and an established operational support model.
  • Application-owned external authority only: defer unless the organization deliberately replaces LiteLLM governance and validates every affected integration path.

Proposed decision

Require PostgreSQL for the production governance plane and manage it as a protected durable dependency. Use distinct runtime and migration privileges, private connectivity and verified transport encryption. Define retention and recovery for each major data category. Treat Redis admission state as coordinated operational state that must reconcile with durable records, not as a substitute for them.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The design gains persistent administration and recovery capability, while database capacity, maintenance and availability become part of the platform's service obligation.
  • Connection limits and write contention can constrain gateway scaling; database schema and encrypted credential recovery must remain aligned with the deployed application version.

Required validation

  • A deployment gate rejects a governed configuration without its required database, and a restore proves keys, permissions and stored provider configuration are usable.
  • Representative concurrency stays within the allocated connection and write budget, with visible behavior when the database rejects or cannot serve requests.

Revisit trigger

Reassess if the organization externalizes governance, changes database operating strategy or demonstrates a bottleneck requiring a different durable-state design for production workloads.
