decisions.body:
Area State and governanceSuggested owner Distributed systems platform leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Workers need shared limits, invalidations and leadership even when response payloads are never cached. Coupling coordination to an optional performance cache can disable important governance state. Its clients, pools and failure behavior therefore need explicit configuration and independent observation.

Options considered

  • Local memory in each worker: reject for a shared enforcement domain because counters and invalidations would depend on request placement.
  • Explicit shared coordination Redis: selected, with separately controlled routing and payload-cache clients and their operational limits.
  • One undifferentiated cache for all purposes: allow only after documenting namespaces, eviction, access and failure coupling between data categories.

Proposed decision

Configure HA Redis for coordination across each enforcement domain, with routing and payload caches managed separately. Keep coordination active when response caching is off. Do not infer shared virtual-key auth caching or a revocation bound from coordination_redis; qualify auth caching and invalidation separately. Specify persistence, eviction, access and connection budgets, separating stores where payload demand could threaten governance.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Shared counters and leadership improve coordination, while virtual-key cache placement and invalidation remain separate behaviors to configure and verify under restart and outage.
  • Separate clients or stores improve operational clarity while increasing configuration surface; flushing a response cache must not inadvertently reset budget or authorization coordination.

Required validation

  • Multiple workers honor the declared shared limit; warmed virtual-key caches on every worker enforce revocation within a separately agreed and measured bound.
  • Disable or flush payload caching and interrupt Redis; auth-cache initialization, invalidation recovery and governance behavior match the explicit configuration rather than inferred coupling.

Revisit trigger

Review when worker count, tenancy, cache volume or Redis failure evidence justifies different partitioning, durability or coordination technology for the production service.

decisions.title: Reserve spending and fail closed on unverifiable budgets
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area State and governanceSuggested owner FinOps and platform controls leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Concurrent requests can appear affordable when checks see only previously recorded spending. Outages and stale counters further weaken admission. The organization must choose its availability-versus-spend tradeoff and distinguish estimable token requests from operations whose complete cost is unknown.

Options considered

  • Recorded-spend checks alone: rejected for bounded production spending because concurrent work can be admitted before previous costs are recorded.
  • Reservation plus fail-closed verification: selected for governed workloads, with explicit estimation and dependency assumptions.
  • Availability-first admission during state failure: permit only as a separately bounded exception with an accountable owner and predefined financial exposure.

Proposed decision

Keep reservation enabled and use fail_closed_budget_enforcement for budget verification, with sensible output limits and current price metadata. Leave database fail-open mode disabled. Because missing or nonpositive estimates skip reservation even with that flag, reject such requests or apply a separately qualified admission rule. Define accepted overshoot exposure and separate controls for batch and media workloads.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Spending controls improve under concurrency and stale-state conditions, but verified admission can reject useful work during coordination or database failures.
  • Missing or nonpositive estimates bypass reservation rather than becoming protected automatically by fail-closed verification; estimation gaps and absent terminal usage need separate admission and reconciliation controls.

Required validation

  • Concurrent expensive requests, stale Redis restoration and database/Redis outages remain within the approved exposure bound and return the documented rejection classes.
  • Requests with missing, zero and negative cost estimates are rejected or demonstrably governed by the separate admission rule; completed and interrupted requests release reservations correctly.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when spending becomes contractual prepayment, new unpriced endpoints enter scope or observed outage cost changes the accepted availability tradeoff.

decisions.title: Reconcile usage and spend as an auditable ledger
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area State and governanceSuggested owner FinOps data engineering leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Gateway estimates, reported usage and invoices can differ through pricing changes, discounts and delayed or missing events. Admission and financial reporting serve different purposes. Spending records should retain uncertainty and reconciliation history instead of presenting every initial estimate as final.

Options considered

  • Treat each gateway estimate as final billing: rejected because estimation and provider accounting need not share timing or scope.
  • Reconciled usage ledger: selected with request/attempt identity, pricing version and explicit correction handling.
  • Provider invoice only: insufficient for timely application attribution and admission, but retain it as an external reconciliation input.

Proposed decision

Record request and attempt identifiers, deployment, observed usage, pricing version, estimated versus final status and correction history in the financial reporting flow. Reconcile gateway totals against provider evidence at an agreed cadence. Define duplicate, late and missing-event handling. Keep admission counters, operational dashboards and financial chargeback related but explicitly separate in meaning.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Finance can explain adjustments and uncertainty, while implementation requires event identity, retention and reconciliation ownership beyond a dashboard showing aggregate spend.
  • Some providers or operations will remain estimates until external evidence arrives; missing usage should be visible rather than silently reported as free consumption.

Required validation

  • Retries, cache hits, cancelled streams and delayed batches produce traceable records without unexplained double counting or silent missing charges.
  • A sampled provider statement reconciles to application totals within an approved tolerance, and corrections preserve the original observation and reason for change.

Revisit trigger

Review when chargeback becomes contractual billing, pricing arrangements change or reconciliation differences exceed the agreed operational and financial tolerance over repeated reporting periods.

decisions.title: Assign authoritative ownership to versioned configuration
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area State and governanceSuggested owner Platform configuration management leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Configuration may arrive through files, environment variables and administrative APIs. Without ownership rules, a restart or UI edit can change effective behavior unexpectedly. The organization needs a reproducible way to determine which source controls global security settings while allowing appropriate team-level administration.

Options considered

  • Unrestricted UI-driven configuration: rejected for global policy because changes and restart behavior would be difficult to reproduce and review.
  • File-owned global configuration with delegated dynamic fields: selected to combine reviewability with bounded team autonomy.
  • Files only for every object: reject where routine key and team administration would create unnecessary deployment coupling.

Proposed decision

Own global route, model, security and dependency configuration through versioned files and reviewed secret references. Declare which team-level fields may change dynamically, who can change them and how they are exported. Test source precedence and prevent drift in protected settings. Emergency changes must be captured back into the authoritative configuration before normal operation resumes.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • In pinned v1.104.0, differing runtime writes and deletion of file-owned settings are rejected; administrative workflows must surface that ownership rather than suggesting an override succeeded.
  • Delegated runtime state needs its own persistence and propagation contract. Resource lists use separate handling and must not inherit assumptions from file-owned scalar settings.

Required validation

  • A restart and fresh deployment reproduce all protected settings from versioned inputs, with expected handling of permitted dynamic state.
  • Differing writes and deletion of file-owned settings are rejected; delegated fields and separately handled resource lists retain their documented persistence and propagation behavior.

Revisit trigger

Review when team autonomy, release cadence or new configuration mechanisms make the current ownership split cumbersome or insufficiently clear for routine administration.

decisions.title: Promote versioned releases with a defined rollback boundary
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Release engineering leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Gateway upgrades can affect adapters, policy behavior, schemas and administrative state simultaneously. Reverting an image does not necessarily revert those other changes. A release process needs to state what can be rolled back safely and what instead requires a forward fix or restored database.

Options considered

  • Rolling upgrade to a moving tag: rejected because the deployed code and reversal target are not reliably reproducible.
  • Versioned staged promotion: selected with known artifacts, configuration changes, compatibility evidence and a release-specific recovery path.
  • Freeze indefinitely on one version: rejected because provider evolution and security support create continuing maintenance requirements.

Proposed decision

Promote an immutable release manifest containing image digests, configuration revisions and migration identity. Run the acceptance corpus in staging and use a controlled traffic increase. Before production, classify rollback as image-only, configuration reversal or coordinated state restore. Keep the previous approved artifact available and establish observable abort criteria for the rollout.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Release decisions become reviewable and recoverable, while maintaining staging and version-specific recovery information adds recurring engineering effort.
  • Some migrations will prevent a simple image rollback; declaring that limitation before deployment avoids discovering it while users are already affected.

Required validation

  • A staging rollback or forward-recovery exercise restores the required API, policy and accounting behavior using the documented release manifest.
  • The rollout stops automatically or operationally when agreed error, latency, policy or accounting criteria are breached, preserving evidence for diagnosis.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when schema compatibility changes, deployment tooling changes or an incident demonstrates that the documented recovery boundary was incomplete for production use.

decisions.title: Choose componentization only where isolation and scale justify it
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Platform deployment architectDate 6 October 2026

Context

The organization has not supplied workload size or an operating model. Separate inference, management and UI services can support independent scaling and exposure policies, but also add routing and lifecycle complexity. A small platform should not inherit extra components without a corresponding operational benefit.

Options considered

  • Monolithic supported deployment: select for a smaller operating team when route restrictions and shared capacity meet its requirements.
  • Componentized gateway, backend and UI: select when independent scaling, exposure or administrative-load isolation provides a measured benefit.
  • Custom service decomposition: reject initially because it creates unverified interfaces and an additional maintenance burden beyond supported deployment shapes.

Proposed decision

Qualify the supported monolith as the simplest production option and the supported componentized deployment as the enterprise expansion option. Choose componentization when required administrative isolation or load behavior justifies it. Preserve the same identity, state and API contract in either shape, and document path routing, component versions and dependency ownership explicitly.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Deployment complexity matches demonstrated requirements, but moving between shapes still requires route and operational regression checks.
  • Component separation can isolate UI or management load, while shared database and Redis dependencies continue to connect the components' availability and security boundaries.

Required validation

  • The selected shape meets inference and administrative workload targets, with every approved route reaching the correct component under failure and upgrade.
  • Where componentization is selected, UI failure and management traffic bursts do not breach the inference service's accepted availability and latency objectives.

Revisit trigger

Review when administrative exposure, traffic growth or operating-team capacity changes enough to justify merging or separating deployment components in the production service.

decisions.title: Bound workers, connection pools and autoscaling together
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Gateway capacity engineering leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Adding replicas or worker processes also adds database and Redis clients, memory use and background activity. Streaming can exhaust concurrency while CPU remains modest. Autoscaling therefore needs a capacity model for dependent services, rather than an isolated target for the gateway's processor utilization.

Options considered

  • Increase workers and replicas independently: rejected because total connections and retained stream resources can exceed state-service capacity.
  • One worker per serving pod initially: selected for simpler scaling and measurement, with bounded per-client pools.
  • CPU-only autoscaling: insufficient as the sole signal where long-lived requests retain capacity without sustained processor usage.

Proposed decision

Start qualification with one serving worker per pod. Set resource limits, stream concurrency and connection pools from measured workloads. Bound maximum replicas against database and Redis capacity, including non-serving clients and operational headroom. Use request/concurrency and latency evidence alongside CPU, and ensure scale-in drains active work according to the stream contract.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Capacity is easier to explain and constrain, while a conservative ceiling may reject excess traffic until additional state-service capacity is provisioned.
  • Multiple clients and background workers need explicit accounting; a healthy gateway CPU graph does not establish available connection, memory or stream capacity.

Required validation

  • A sustained mixed workload and burst produce stable memory, bounded connections and acceptable queueing through scale-out and scale-in transitions.
  • Maximum permitted replica count does not exceed dependent-service limits, and long streams remain correctly drained when capacity contracts.

Revisit trigger

Reassess after workload shape changes, a measured capacity bottleneck or evidence that multiple workers per pod improve efficiency without weakening limits.

decisions.title: Export metadata-focused telemetry through bounded paths
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Observability platform leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Operators need enough information to distinguish gateway faults, provider latency and policy rejection, but unrestricted prompt logging creates additional sensitive copies. Telemetry failures can also consume resources or slow inference. The reference service needs a useful diagnostic contract with controlled content, capacity and retention.

Options considered

  • Full request and response capture everywhere: rejected as the default because it increases sensitive-data exposure and storage volume.
  • Metadata-focused telemetry: selected with request identity, attempts, timing, usage and outcomes, plus controlled content debugging when necessary.
  • Disable all telemetry: rejected because failures, lost accounting and policy gaps would become difficult to diagnose and verify.

Proposed decision

Export request and attempt IDs, tenant references, resolved deployment, timings, usage and categorized outcomes by default. Redact prompt and response bodies and restrict raw-request debugging. Bound callback timeouts, queues and label cardinality. Define visible behavior for sink failure, and make any temporary content capture time-limited, approved and routed to a restricted destination.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Operators retain actionable evidence while reducing payload duplication, but some debugging requires a controlled replay or specifically authorized content capture.
  • Telemetry can lag or drop according to its declared delivery contract; dashboards must expose queue saturation and missing events instead of implying completeness.

Required validation

  • Synthetic secrets and personal-data markers are absent from normal success, error, stream, retry and metrics exports, including exceptional raw-request paths.
  • A stalled telemetry sink does not cause unbounded memory or breach the chosen inference behavior; drops, retries and queue pressure remain visible.

Revisit trigger

Review when incidents cannot be diagnosed from retained metadata, a new sink is introduced or privacy and retention requirements change materially.

decisions.title: Preserve attributable administrative audit with separate retention
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Security monitoring and audit leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Changes to keys, policy and provider configuration need a history independent of ordinary inference diagnostics. Shared administrative credentials and caller-controlled attribution weaken that history. Audit records also have different readers and retention requirements from prompt logs, so combining their storage and access policies is undesirable.

Options considered

  • Inference logs as the only audit source: rejected because they do not establish complete administrative change history or responsibility.
  • Dedicated administrative audit flow: selected with named actors, protected retention and separate access from routine diagnostics.
  • Keep audit solely in the mutable application database: insufficient where tamper resistance, investigation continuity or independent retention is required.

Proposed decision

Capture administrative changes with authenticated actor, operation, target, time and a suitably redacted change description. Export to a separately restricted audit destination and assign retention through organizational policy. Permit attribution overrides only for specifically authorized delegation. Verify delivery and gaps without claiming tamper-proof or complete history merely because an audit feature is enabled.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Investigations can separate administrative changes from inference events, while retention, access reviews and delivery monitoring create a distinct operational responsibility.
  • Audit data may contain sensitive configuration or identifiers and must be minimized; an unavailable audit sink needs an agreed response for high-impact administrative operations.

Required validation

  • Key, role, model and budget changes produce attributable records that a normal workload caller cannot forge through request metadata or headers.
  • A controlled export outage exposes a detectable gap or retry state, and authorized reviewers can retrieve retained records after application database restoration.

Revisit trigger

Review when regulatory retention, delegation workflows or incident evidence requires stronger durability, integrity controls or a different administrative failure policy.

Dependencies ADR-008 · ADR-025

Dedicated administrative audit flow: selected with named actors, protected retention and separate access from routine diagnostics. Keep audit solely in the mutable application database: insufficient where tamper resistance, investigation continuity or independent retention is required. Proposed decision Capture administrative changes with authenticated actor, operation, target, time and a suitably redacted change description. Export to a separately restricted audit destination and assign retention through organizational policy. Permit attribution overrides only for specifically authorized delegation. Verify delivery and gaps without claiming tamper-proof or complete history merely because an audit feature is enabled. Consequences and tradeoffs Investigations can separate administrative changes from inference events, while retention, access reviews and delivery monitoring create a distinct operational responsibility. Audit data may contain sensitive configuration or identifiers and must be minimized; an unavailable audit sink needs an agreed response for high-impact administrative operations. Required validation Key, role, model and budget changes produce attributable records that a normal workload caller cannot forge through request metadata or headers. A controlled export outage exposes a detectable gap or retry state, and authorized reviewers can retrieve retained records after application database restoration. Revisit trigger Review when regulatory retention, delegation workflows or incident evidence requires stronger durability, integrity controls or a different administrative failure policy. decisions.title: Apply database schemas through one controlled migration job
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Database release ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Multiple replicas starting simultaneously should not independently decide how to change durable shared state. A schema change also needs privileges different from routine request processing. The release process must coordinate migrations, application compatibility and recovery while keeping schema mutation out of ordinary pod startup.

Options considered

  • Migrate from every serving pod: rejected because rollout concurrency and elevated runtime privilege complicate control and failure recovery.
  • One version-matched migration job: selected as a gated release operation with explicit privileges and backup preparation.
  • Manual ad hoc database edits: rejected as a normal path because drift is difficult to reproduce and reconcile with application migration history.

Proposed decision

Disable automatic schema updates on serving instances and run one controlled migration job for the shared database. Match the job to the promoted application release, inspect changes and establish backup/recovery readiness first. Prevent application rollout when migration fails. Validate mixed-version compatibility or choose a coordinated maintenance sequence when it cannot be assured.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Schema changes have one observable owner and gate, but a failed migration can legitimately delay the release until recovery is understood.
  • A successful migration command does not establish absence of schema drift or safe downgrade; those assumptions need separate review and evidence.

Required validation

  • Simultaneous deployment attempts cannot run conflicting migrations, and failure of the migration job prevents the new serving version from receiving traffic.
  • A restored database and chosen recovery artifact successfully process required transactions after a deliberately failed or incompatible staging migration.

Revisit trigger

Reassess for a breaking schema change, multiple regional release pipelines or tooling that changes migration locking and application compatibility guarantees.

decisions.title: Separate process health, readiness and graceful draining
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Site reliability leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A running process, reachable database and successful model request describe different kinds of health. Using one probe for all of them can cause restart storms or route traffic to an unusable service. Shutdown must also account for long-lived streams and pending asynchronous accounting work.

Options considered

  • One end-to-end probe for every lifecycle decision: rejected because provider or shared-state failure can unnecessarily restart healthy processes.
  • Separate liveness, readiness and synthetic service checks: selected, with outcomes aligned to the chosen dependency failure policy.
  • Immediate termination on rollout: rejected where it would cut streams and abandon accounting without a documented application recovery path.

Proposed decision

Use process liveness to identify a stuck runtime, readiness to express whether the instance should accept new work, and synthetic checks to observe the complete user path. Align load-balancer and DNS decisions with the selected fail policy. Drain new admissions before termination and bound the time allowed for active streams and queued work to finish.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Failures can be diagnosed and contained more precisely, while probe design becomes part of the service contract rather than a copied deployment default.
  • Long-running requests can extend rollout or scale-in time; after the agreed drain deadline, clients and accounting must follow a declared incomplete-work procedure.

Required validation

  • Provider failure does not trigger an unnecessary process restart, while loss of required authorization state produces the intended readiness and routing result.
  • During rollout and scale-in, new work stops, existing streams finish or terminate as specified, and remaining queued work is accounted for visibly.

Revisit trigger

Review when dependency failure policy, ingress behavior or new long-lived protocols change what the service should admit during degradation and shutdown.

decisions.title: Establish multi-zone availability before regional expansion
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Infrastructure resilience leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A second region is not automatically the simplest answer to instance or zone failure. It introduces data, coordination and recovery choices beyond replica placement. The organization should first remove local single points of failure and establish measurable objectives before committing to a more complex regional topology.

Options considered

  • One instance and one zone: reject for the reference production service unless the business explicitly accepts the resulting outage exposure.
  • Multiple zones within one approved region: selected as the initial availability baseline with resilient state services.
  • Immediate multi-region deployment: defer until agreed recovery or locality requirements justify its added coordination, data and operating complexity.

Proposed decision

Spread serving capacity across failure zones and use appropriately resilient managed PostgreSQL and Redis configurations. Reserve capacity for a zone loss and align disruption controls with that design. Define business-approved availability, recovery-time and recovery-point objectives before regional expansion; treat these values as requirements to agree and test, not capabilities assumed from replica count.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Common local failures can be handled with less complexity than a global topology, but a region-wide event still requires a deliberate recovery plan.
  • Resilience consumes standby capacity and operational attention; replicas do not protect against shared configuration mistakes, compromised credentials or unrecoverable encrypted state.

Required validation

  • A controlled zone-loss exercise maintains the accepted capacity and behavior while database and Redis failover complete within approved recovery objectives.
  • Loss of one serving replica, planned maintenance and disruption-budget behavior do not combine to remove all healthy capacity from service.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when region outage exposure, user geography or contractual recovery requirements exceed what the qualified single-region design can provide with acceptable risk.

decisions.title: Allocate quotas by regional enforcement domain
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Global platform and FinOps architectDate 6 October 2026

Context

Geographically distributed gateways can share durable records while making admission decisions through separate regional coordination stores. That arrangement favors latency but does not automatically provide one atomic global quota. The organization must define whether limits apply per region, globally or through explicit allocations.

Options considered

  • Regional limits presented as global: rejected because simultaneous regional traffic could exceed the expectation communicated to application owners.
  • Regional quota allocations with reconciliation: selected when regional latency and isolation matter more than a fungible global pool.
  • One global coordination domain: consider for strict global admission, accepting cross-region latency and a larger common dependency.

Proposed decision

Before enabling additional regions, partition capacity and spending allowances into explicit regional allocations whose sum respects the approved global envelope. Document redistribution and failover rules and reconcile global usage separately. If strict globally shared admission is mandatory, qualify a common coordinator and its partition behavior instead of relying on a shared database alone.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Applications receive honest regional and global limit semantics, but unused allocation may remain stranded until an authorized rebalance occurs.
  • Failover can create sudden demand in the surviving region; capacity and budget must be reserved or transferred deliberately without briefly granting both regions the same allowance.

Required validation

  • Simultaneous regional load and network partitions remain within the declared combined exposure, with no hidden multiplication of quota after failover.
  • An allocation transfer has a traceable owner and does not authorize overlapping excess capacity; global reconciliation identifies delayed or missing regional usage.

Revisit trigger

Review when regional traffic imbalance, latency goals or contractual spending rules justify changing from allocated limits to a shared global admission service.

decisions.title: Recover configuration, durable state and encryption material together
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Disaster recovery ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Container recovery is insufficient when keys, policy, usage or provider credentials remain unavailable. Database state, encryption material and configuration must be compatible. Restoring older state can also reintroduce revoked access or stale counters, requiring security and accounting reconciliation.

Options considered

  • Database backups alone: rejected because restored encrypted credentials and effective configuration may remain unusable or inconsistent.
  • Coordinated recovery set: selected with versioned configuration, authorized encryption material, database recovery and post-restore reconciliation.
  • Live replica as the only recovery mechanism: rejected because it can reproduce corruption, mistaken policy changes or malicious mutations.

Proposed decision

Maintain a recovery manifest linking database recovery points, application versions, configuration revisions and authorized secret recovery. Rehearse restoration into isolation, including credential decryption and access reconciliation. Rebuild disposable payload caches rather than treating them as authoritative. Define handling for buffered spend, revoked identities and provider resources created after the restored point.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Recovery can be measured as a complete service outcome, but protected access to backup encryption material and historical configuration requires deliberate governance.
  • Restoration may temporarily disagree with external provider activity or recent administrative changes; the service should not resume until accepted reconciliation and access checks are complete.

Required validation

  • An isolated restore authenticates approved workloads, denies known revoked access and successfully uses stored credentials without depending on unrecovered live infrastructure.
  • Timed recovery records achieved RTO/RPO, missing or replayed spend and external resource discrepancies, with explicit approval before recovered traffic is accepted.

Revisit trigger

Repeat after material schema, encryption, identity or topology changes and whenever a recovery exercise reveals an assumption absent from the manifest.

decisions.title: Verify artifact provenance and maintain an active patch process
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Software supply-chain security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A gateway holds valuable credentials while providers and software evolve rapidly. Package names and mutable tags do not establish reproducible content. Artifact approval must work alongside vulnerability response because neither indefinite version freezing nor automatic upgrading provides sufficient assurance.

Options considered

  • Automatically deploy the newest package or rolling tag: rejected because origin, content and behavioral changes are not reviewed before production.
  • Verified immutable artifacts with staged promotion: selected, alongside advisory monitoring and an assigned emergency patch owner.
  • Long upgrade delays as the primary defense: rejected because delay neither proves artifact safety nor preserves security support indefinitely.

Proposed decision

Pin approved image digests and verify signatures against an independently controlled trust root before promotion. Record dependency and advisory assessment with each release. Track the supplier's current supported-version window and apply urgent fixes through an expedited version of the same pipeline. Revalidate signing-key changes and never interpret a valid signature as proof of secure code.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Deployments become reproducible and their origin reviewable, while the platform must continuously fund compatibility qualification, advisory triage and trust-root maintenance.
  • Provenance controls reduce certain supply-chain risks but cannot eliminate a compromised trusted build or application vulnerability; runtime isolation and incident response remain necessary.

Required validation

  • Unsigned, unexpected-digest and unapproved artifacts fail the deployment gate, while the approved image is traceable to its release and review evidence.
  • An advisory simulation identifies affected deployments, produces a qualified replacement and exercises rollback or forward recovery within the organization's response objective.

Revisit trigger

Reopen after a supplier incident, signing or publishing change, altered support policy or evidence that patch response no longer meets organizational risk requirements.

decisions.title: Control callbacks and extensions as privileged code
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Gateway application security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Custom hooks inspect requests, modify responses and access runtime context. They introduce dependencies, destinations and failure modes outside the standard contract. Extensions should therefore be treated as privileged application code in a credential-bearing service, with explicit ownership and review.

Options considered

  • Unreviewed in-process extensions: rejected because they inherit powerful access and can alter every participating application's behavior.
  • Reviewed, versioned minimal callbacks: selected only where documented configuration cannot meet the required behavior.
  • External narrow policy services: prefer when isolation is worth the network dependency, with explicit timeout and failure contracts.

Proposed decision

Prefer documented configuration over custom execution. For necessary callbacks, assign an owner, review dependencies and data access, pin code with the release manifest and bound execution time. Restrict outbound destinations and secrets. Use an isolated external service for high-risk logic when feasible, and prohibit request-controlled imports, code or arbitrary command selection.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Extensions remain possible without becoming an uncontrolled platform surface, but custom requirements now carry ongoing testing and support obligations.
  • Externalizing logic can improve privilege separation while introducing latency and availability dependencies; in-process code cannot be presumed sandboxed merely because it uses a plugin interface.

Required validation

  • A failing or hanging callback produces the selected timeout, rejection or telemetry behavior without unbounded resources or unauthorized payload export.
  • The release inventory identifies every extension and dependency, and synthetic request fields cannot select executable code or expand its permitted destinations.

Revisit trigger

Review when an extension's scope grows, its owner changes, a standard capability replaces it or an incident exposes unacceptable in-process privileges.

decisions.title: Default-deny MCP access and isolate tool execution
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Agent platform security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Tool gateways can access external systems and perform actions, creating trust relationships beyond text generation. Permissions, upstream credentials and tool descriptions all matter. Empty-list and inheritance behavior must be understood before model credentials gain discovery or execution authority.

Options considered

  • Enable every configured MCP server for all keys: rejected because ordinary model access should not imply unrelated tool authority.
  • Explicit server/tool grants in an isolated execution boundary: selected, with application authorization for consequential actions.
  • Run arbitrary stdio tools inside the main gateway: rejected initially because executable dependencies would share a valuable credential-bearing runtime.

Proposed decision

Disable unused MCP routes and leave stdio execution off in the main gateway. When tools are required, grant explicit server and tool entitlements, use clear deny-all semantics and isolate execution and credentials. Constrain arguments, review or pin tool catalogs where supported, and apply default-on input/result policy without relying on inherited parent-request guardrail selection.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Model access and tool authority remain separate, but onboarding tools requires permission design, upstream credential ownership and a larger application acceptance matrix.
  • Gateway checks cannot undo a completed external action or replace the target system's resource authorization; consequential actions still need appropriate application approval and recovery.

Required validation

  • A model-only key discovers and executes zero tools, while an approved tool identity can use only its listed servers, operations and argument scope.
  • Changed catalogs, poisoned results, absent guards and disabled stdio calls follow the declared policy; HTTP-success tool-error envelopes are recorded as failures.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when introducing new tool categories, executable transports, external user delegation or actions with materially different side effects and recovery requirements.

decisions.body:
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Stateful API integration leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Files, jobs, conversations and prior-response identifiers represent provider-side state. Similar endpoint names do not make those resources interchangeable. Follow-up requests must preserve the resource's tenant and origin when they are retried, polled, continued, transferred between replicas or deleted.

Options considered

  • Route stateful follow-ups like ordinary stateless completions: rejected because another deployment may not own or understand the resource.
  • Explicit origin and tenant binding: selected for every retained identifier, with a defined lifecycle and failure outcome.
  • Application-managed provider state: acceptable where intentional, but document the reduced portability and prevent unvalidated identifiers from crossing tenants.

Proposed decision

Track or reliably encode the tenant, provider, deployment and relevant region associated with stateful resources. Route continuation, polling and deletion to a compatible owner. Disable generic fallback where ownership cannot be preserved. Define retention, expiration, recovery and orphan cleanup, and document which workflows require application mediation rather than transparent gateway substitution.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Stateful operations become predictable and isolated, but their portability is narrower than the portability of simple text generation.
  • Resource ownership information may need durable retention, and provider outages can make continuation unavailable even while another provider can serve new stateless requests.

Required validation

  • Create, poll, continue and delete representative resources across replicas; each operation reaches the correct provider and rejects another tenant's identifier.
  • Provider failover and gateway restoration produce a documented result for existing resources, with no accidental new resource or silent loss of ownership.

Revisit trigger

Review when adding another stateful endpoint, changing identifier translation or adopting a provider-independent application store for conversations and job lifecycle.

decisions.title: Govern batch and media work with distinct admission rules
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Asynchronous workload platform leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Batch and media work can differ substantially from chat in cost, duration and payload size. A small submission may authorize a much larger workload. Admission must therefore understand total exposure rather than reuse token estimates that cannot represent the operation.

Options considered

  • Apply the chat budget policy unchanged: rejected where the gateway cannot estimate the complete asynchronous or media workload at admission.
  • Separate batch/media admission: selected with workload estimates, payload constraints, concurrency and completion reconciliation.
  • Disable these endpoints permanently: reject as a blanket rule, but keep them outside the initial contract until a required use case is qualified.

Proposed decision

Create separate service classes for batch and media operations. Require a bounded workload declaration or application-side estimate, constrain file and output sizes, and limit outstanding jobs and submission rate. Define cancellation and eventual-cost behavior. Admit only approved provider operations and reconcile final usage when completion evidence arrives, making uncertain estimates visible.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Large delayed workloads cannot silently inherit chat's assumptions, while applications may need a submission workflow and an asynchronous status experience.
  • Some costs remain uncertain until completion or provider billing; cancellation may limit future work without reversing work already performed or charges already incurred.

Required validation

  • An oversized or underestimated batch/media request is rejected or escalated before accepted exposure exceeds its approved service-class envelope.
  • Delayed completion, failed jobs, cancellation and duplicate polling produce consistent resource ownership and accounting without repeatedly charging the submission estimate.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when a provider changes pricing or cancellation semantics, a new modality enters scope or workload estimates consistently miss accepted exposure limits.

decisions.title: Keep application quality and evaluation ownership with product teams
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Application product and evaluation leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Authenticated, correctly routed requests can still produce unusable answers. Quality depends on prompts, retrieval, task context and downstream handling beyond gateway control. Model abstraction should preserve clear product accountability rather than implicitly assigning answer quality to infrastructure operators.

Options considered

  • Treat HTTP success and provider compatibility as quality acceptance: rejected because they do not measure whether the application achieved its task.
  • Application-owned evaluation with shared platform tooling: selected to connect model changes to user outcomes and risk.
  • Central platform approves every application's answers: reject as the sole model because domain expertise and product accountability remain with application owners.

Proposed decision

Require each production application to own a representative evaluation corpus, acceptance criteria and regression review for its model aliases. Evaluate prompt, retrieval, fallback and tool behavior together where they affect outcomes. The platform provides traces and controlled rollout support, while application owners approve material model substitutions and safely validate generated content before downstream use.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Infrastructure and product responsibilities remain clear, but application teams must budget for evaluations and maintain representative data as user needs change.
  • A routing or provider upgrade may be operationally healthy yet blocked from application adoption until task quality, safety and structured-output expectations are accepted.

Required validation

  • A proposed model or fallback change passes application-specific quality and structured-output checks, including the failure cases most consequential to that product.
  • Production monitoring can distinguish gateway success from application task failure and triggers a controlled rollback or review when quality regresses.

Revisit trigger

Review when the application's task, user population, retrieval data or risk level changes enough to make its evaluation corpus unrepresentative.

Dependencies ADR-004 · ADR-014 · ADR-025

decisions.title: Contract explicitly for required entitlements and support
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Commercial and lifecycleSuggested owner Platform product owner and procurement leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Adoption combines software capability, licensing and operating responsibility. Documentation may describe differently entitled or immature features. Installing the gateway does not establish that identity, governance and support requirements are covered; the chosen artifact and agreement must be assessed together.

Options considered

  • OSS with organization-owned supplementary controls: select when internal capability and total operating cost satisfy the actual requirements.
  • Enterprise subscription: select when required native controls and contracted support justify cost and reduce a measured operational burden.
  • Assume all documented features and support are included: rejected because entitlement and response commitments must be verified for the chosen agreement.

Proposed decision

Build a version-specific inventory of required controls, their edition, deployment constraints and contract terms. Compare OSS integration work, Enterprise subscription and managed alternatives using total operating cost. Confirm support hours, escalation, response commitments, release support and offline-license behavior. Assign renewal ownership and avoid making an unqualified beta feature a mandatory production dependency.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Procurement reflects the real operating model, but both technical and commercial assumptions need periodic review as usage and requirements evolve.
  • A license does not transfer responsibility for local configuration, data handling or all incidents; support value depends on the actual agreement and operational collaboration.

Required validation

  • The selected artifact and agreement demonstrably enable every required feature, and a support exercise reaches the intended escalation path with correct account details.
  • A controlled nonproduction expiry or license-service outage establishes the affected functions and recovery procedure without relying on undocumented continuity assumptions.

Revisit trigger

Reassess before renewal, after major volume or regulatory changes, and whenever entitlement, supported-version policy or required support response changes for the service.

decisions.title: Qualify performance and SLOs with realistic traffic
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Commercial and lifecycleSuggested owner Performance and service reliability leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Overhead depends on request shape, concurrency, providers and enabled controls. Isolated benchmarks cannot predict the complete enterprise path. With no supplied traffic profile or objectives, performance claims remain hypotheses until stakeholders agree a representative workload and measurable service requirements.

Options considered

  • Adopt vendor throughput numbers as production capacity: rejected because hardware, features, providers and request distributions may differ materially.
  • Representative qualification with a direct-provider baseline: selected to separate gateway overhead from provider and application behavior.
  • Optimize only average latency: reject as insufficient for streaming, tail behavior, budget admission, failures and resource saturation.

Proposed decision

Agree traffic classes and proposed SLOs with application owners, then benchmark the exact release, topology and enabled controls. Measure gateway overhead, first output, full completion, tail latency, error categories and resource use separately. Include streaming, long prompts, burst traffic and dependency faults. Publish capacity with configuration, methodology and limits rather than a universal performance claim.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Capacity planning and comparative evaluation become reproducible, while qualification requires representative test data, provider cost and controlled measurement effort.
  • Higher throughput is not automatically better if it weakens policy or increases dropped accounting; operational and correctness gates remain part of performance acceptance.

Required validation

  • Repeated runs of the declared workload meet agreed latency, availability and resource targets with governance enabled, and include a reproducible direct-provider comparison.
  • Load beyond the accepted envelope produces controlled admission and recovery rather than unbounded queues, memory growth or unexplained loss of accounting and traces.

Revisit trigger

Repeat when release, runtime, hardware, controls, provider mix or workload distribution changes enough to invalidate the previously measured capacity and service objectives.

decisions.title: Maintain an exit strategy and explicit decision lifecycle
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Commercial and lifecycleSuggested owner Enterprise architecture review boardDate 6 October 2026

Context

A gateway can reduce provider coupling while introducing its own control and data dependencies. Adoption should remain reversible at a known cost. These records are proposals, so decision governance must clearly distinguish evaluation intent from accepted organizational commitments.

Options considered

  • Adopt every gateway-specific interface without an exit plan: rejected because migration cost and unsupported assumptions would remain unknown.
  • Own contracts, exports and evaluation evidence: selected to preserve a practicable replacement path and accountable decision history.
  • Avoid all vendor-specific capability: reject as unnecessarily restrictive when a useful feature's migration cost is understood and explicitly accepted.

Proposed decision

Own the external API and alias contracts, identity mapping, configuration exports and evaluation corpus. Inventory proprietary features and retained resource dependencies, and rehearse one representative application migration to an alternative. Keep every ADR Proposed until the responsible organization accepts it with evidence, owner and date; supersede records explicitly when assumptions or decisions change.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The organization can compare replacement costs and avoid confusing a report with approved policy, while maintaining exports and migration exercises requires continuing effort.
  • Some stateful resources or enterprise features will remain costly to migrate; that cost becomes an explicit accepted dependency rather than a hidden portability promise.

Required validation

  • A representative application uses the replacement path without obtaining unrestricted provider credentials, and required policy, quality and reporting behavior remain demonstrable.
  • Exported configuration and governance data are readable independently; each accepted or superseded ADR links its owner, evidence, date and related operational changes.

Revisit trigger

Review at renewal, after a major incident or supplier change, and whenever accepted assumptions no longer describe the organization's actual service.

Dependencies ADR-003 · ADR-004 · ADR-020 · ADR-021 · ADR-035 · ADR-037 · ADR-038 · ADR-039

decisions.title: Select the edition and pin a complete release unit
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Platform boundarySuggested owner AI platform ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

The assessment pins an OSS transport release, while Enterprise publishes an independently versioned distribution. Shared code is evidence about that public base, not acceptance evidence for a private Enterprise artifact. A service commitment needs an identifiable implementation and accountable operator.

Options considered

  • Selected: an explicit edition and immutable release bundle, with a named service owner and recorded dependencies.
  • Rejected: latest tags, because an unreviewed deployment can change authentication, schemas and extensions together.
  • Deferred: Enterprise procurement until its OSS base, support scope and operational obligations are documented.

Proposed decision

Qualify OSS 2.2.6 as the public implementation baseline. Adopt Enterprise only where synchronized governance or licensed controls justify it, and record its exact image, OSS base, chart, configuration and plugins. Treat every production version change as a new release unit with a reviewed compatibility and rollback record.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • A reproducible baseline improves incident attribution but requires artifact inventory and disciplined update work.
  • Edition selection remains conditional; no private Enterprise binary or contractual capability is accepted by this report.

Required validation

  • Release inventory resolves every image and extension to immutable identifiers and identifies its owner.
  • A clean deployment reconstructs the approved effective configuration without downloading mutable executable artifacts.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a required feature changes edition, the vendor rebases Enterprise, or the maintained release can no longer satisfy support or security obligations.

Dependencies None; foundational decision.

decisions.title: Publish a bounded endpoint, alias and resource contract
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Platform boundarySuggested owner API product ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

A compatibility gateway can expose more operations than a service is ready to support. Applications also depend on model behavior, retained resource identifiers and asynchronous results. The supported contract must therefore be narrower and more precise than a list of recognizable endpoint names.

Options considered

  • Selected: a versioned capability matrix and logical aliases for approved application workloads.
  • Rejected: blanket compatibility promises based solely on successful chat examples or provider counts.
  • Deferred: stateful, realtime, batch and large-media surfaces until their complete lifecycle is qualified.

Proposed decision

Start with explicitly tested inference families and versioned logical aliases. Document parameters, errors, streaming semantics, provider ownership and allowed fallback targets. Admit files, batch, media and retained responses through separate workload classes, with authorization on every subsequent read, update and deletion and a documented provider-pinning rule. Keep business-critical asynchronous work in an external durable workflow until replay and recovery are qualified.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Application teams gain a stable contract while provider-specific features require deliberate additions.
  • Some direct-provider clients need adapters, and a stored object may constrain later routing or migration.

Required validation

  • The contract corpus covers success, unsupported parameters, errors and terminal streaming behavior for each approved alias.
  • Cross-identity resource access fails throughout creation, polling, retrieval and deletion; large jobs cannot exhaust interactive admission. Test process death and duplicate submission.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a new endpoint family, model capability, retained-object workflow or compatibility shim is requested and an accountable application owner supplies qualification evidence.

Dependencies BIF-ADR-001

decisions.title: Require attributable workload credentials on every inference surface
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and isolationSuggested owner Identity engineering leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Fresh inference authentication defaults are stronger in the assessed release, but saved choices can survive an upgrade. Credential options and opt-in direct provider keys complicate attribution. A shared service needs an explicit policy that remains effective across different transport and application paths.

Options considered

  • Selected: distinct workload and environment credentials linked to accountable policy owners.
  • Rejected: anonymous inference or shared administrator credentials for applications, because ownership and revocation become ambiguous.
  • Rejected: direct provider-key injection for the reference service, which weakens the intended registered-key boundary.

Proposed decision

Explicitly enable inference authentication and disable direct-key access. Issue narrowly scoped workload credentials, constrain accepted credential forms, and reject conflicting identity headers. Maintain an inventory of keys, owners, expiry and rotation procedures. Establish a separate authenticated bootstrap for administration; setup tokens never become application credentials.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Workload attribution supports incident containment and chargeback but increases credential lifecycle responsibilities.
  • A shared workload key still requires application-level user authorization and cannot establish per-user resource isolation alone.

Required validation

  • Fresh, migrated and restored instances reject missing, invalid, revoked and conflicting credentials on every enabled surface.
  • Raw provider credentials cannot bypass the approved policy; accepted calls retain a stable workload identity through retries.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when federated workload identity, delegated user tokens or a new transport is added, or observed revocation exceeds the agreed bound.

Dependencies BIF-ADR-001 · BIF-ADR-002

A shared workload key still requires application-level user authorization and cannot establish per-user resource isolation alone. Raw provider credentials cannot bypass the approved policy; accepted calls retain a stable workload identity through retries. decisions.title: Separate private administration from workforce inference access
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and isolationSuggested owner Security architecture leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Management authority can change providers, identity mappings and executable integrations. Enterprise identity synchronization also has multiple authority paths and caches. A login that succeeds is insufficient evidence that offboarding and least privilege behave as the organization intends.

Options considered

  • Selected: private administration with role-specific privileges and an authoritative identity lifecycle.
  • Rejected: broad developer administrator roles, because configuration and executable changes share a large impact radius.
  • Deferred: mixed OIDC and SCIM authority until removal, precedence and partial-claim behavior are qualified.

Proposed decision

Keep administrative routes behind a private access boundary and corporate identity. Define custom roles for operations, security, application onboarding and audit. Select one authoritative provisioning mode, test issuer and audience validation, and require explicit offboarding that revokes sessions and derived credentials across all replicas within an agreed bound.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The organization gains accountable change authority but must operate identity mappings and a recovery account.
  • Emergency access remains possible through a separately protected procedure that records actor, purpose, duration and subsequent review.

Required validation

  • A role matrix denies unauthorized direct API operations, including plugin, provider, identity and audit-retention changes.
  • Offboarding tests include omitted claims, stale sessions, SCIM interruption, JWKS rotation and isolated replicas.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when IdP topology, provisioning authority or Enterprise identity behavior changes, and whenever an access incident exposes an unbounded revocation interval.

decisions.title: Prove ownership and tenancy beyond role permissions
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Identity and isolationSuggested owner Data security ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Operational permission and row visibility solve different problems. Legacy unowned resources and ownerless credentials create exceptions to ordinary team scoping. Multiple entitlement profiles may also widen effective access. Tenant claims must be justified across all participating resources and migration paths.

Options considered

  • Selected: explicit ownership, scoped roles and adversarial resource-access qualification.
  • Rejected: assuming dashboard filtering or a customer label provides complete tenant isolation.
  • Selected for stronger boundaries: separate deployments and credentials where shared-process policy cannot meet the data classification.

Proposed decision

Assign an owner and tenant scope to every supported resource before shared production use. Restrict workspace-wide credentials, review cumulative profile grants, and migrate legacy unowned rows deliberately. Test caches, prompts, logs, exports, tools and retained provider objects as separate isolation surfaces; use physical separation where required.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Fine-grained sharing is possible, but legacy imports and profile changes become security-sensitive migrations.
  • Separate deployments increase cost and operations while reducing dependence on a shared application's row-filtering correctness.

Required validation

  • Two adversarial tenants cannot read, mutate, enumerate or export each other's resources using guessed identifiers.
  • Restored legacy records and users with several profiles retain only the documented effective visibility.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a new resource type, profile-sharing pattern, acquisition or regulated workload expands the tenancy boundary or invalidates existing isolation evidence.

Dependencies BIF-ADR-003 · BIF-ADR-004

decisions.title: Own configuration sections and reconcile changes deliberately
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Configuration and secretsSuggested owner Platform configuration ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

File configuration, stored runtime edits and authoritative startup reconciliation can produce different effective states. An omitted section differs from an explicitly empty section. A repeatable deployment must specify who owns each entity and when a stored change should survive or be removed.

Options considered

  • Selected: explicit section ownership and reviewed configuration bundles with effective-state comparisons.
  • Rejected: unmanaged mixing of dashboard edits and deployment files, which obscures drift and rollback intent.
  • Selected selectively: authoritative file reconciliation only for sections whose deletion semantics have been qualified.

Proposed decision

Record ownership for each configuration section and choose split or authoritative mode deliberately. Restrict runtime edits to authorized workflows, export their effective state, and review pruning before restart. Package configuration with the release and verify node convergence; do not treat startup reconciliation as a runtime write-protection mechanism.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Operators can retain legitimate runtime administration while keeping a reviewable desired state.
  • Authoritative empty sections can remove stored entities; recovery therefore needs previous effective configuration and database state.

Required validation

  • A restored staging database demonstrates unchanged-file, changed-file, missing-section and empty-section outcomes.
  • Every serving node reports the intended policy after rollout, and unauthorized management edits fail.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when configuration ownership changes, a section gains new reconciliation semantics, or an incident reveals drift that the current comparison cannot detect.

Dependencies BIF-ADR-001 · BIF-ADR-004

decisions.title: Separate provider rotation from encryption-key recovery
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Configuration and secretsSuggested owner Secrets management ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Provider credentials, virtual keys, external-vault references and database encryption keys have different lifecycles. An encryption-key change is not equivalent to updating a provider secret. Recovery must preserve the material needed to decrypt retained state without granting unnecessary write authority to the gateway.

Options considered

  • Selected: externally managed secrets with read-only access and a separately protected encryption key.
  • Rejected: plaintext secrets embedded in reusable configuration, diagnostics or deployment history.
  • Deferred: automatic gateway-owned vault writes and deletion until ownership and recovery consequences are accepted.

Proposed decision

Use workload identity and read-only vault retrieval where supported. Record secret refresh and flush behavior and verify rotation across replicas. Protect database encryption material with the backup recovery process, test sensitive-field coverage, and require a separately rehearsed re-encryption or rebuild procedure before changing the encryption key.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Secret custody improves while vault outages and refresh delay become explicit service dependencies.
  • Backups can remain unreadable without the protected key; broad secret-manager write privileges would enlarge incident impact.

Required validation

  • Rotation proves the last use of an old provider credential, including a node that missed invalidation.
  • Restore succeeds with authorized encryption material, fails safely with the wrong key, and exposes no cleartext secrets in diagnostics.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a secret backend, encryption implementation, rotation requirement or supported online re-encryption procedure changes, or a recovery exercise exposes incomplete key custody.

Dependencies BIF-ADR-004 · BIF-ADR-006

decisions.title: Enforce destination and residency policy outside request content
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Configuration and secretsSuggested owner Network security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Provider URLs, remote assets, configuration catalogs, proxy settings and tools can all cause outbound connections. Software URL checks address individual paths, while authorized administrators may still configure legitimate private endpoints. Residency and internal-network protection need an independent, auditable network policy.

Options considered

  • Selected: destination-specific egress allowlists and separate internal-model network policy.
  • Rejected: unrestricted outbound access based only on application URL validation.
  • Rejected: a region label as evidence of residency, because traffic and retained data can leave through other integrations.

Proposed decision

Allow approved provider, vault, IdP, storage, telemetry and tool destinations through controlled egress. Block metadata and unrelated private services, validate TLS and trusted proxy headers, and review every dial-target change. Include caches, guardrail processors and backups in residency decisions; pin offline catalogs where external retrieval is unnecessary.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Defense remains effective if a request-processing path fails its own URL checks.
  • Private model hosting and external integrations require deliberate network exceptions and continued ownership of those exceptions.

Required validation

  • Controlled URL-fetch tests cannot reach unauthorized internal recorders through redirects, alternate address families or DNS changes.
  • Authenticated configuration changes cannot violate network policy, and all permitted data destinations match the residency inventory.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a provider, region, private model endpoint, tool server or external evaluator changes the actual network graph or data-processing jurisdiction.

Dependencies BIF-ADR-005 · BIF-ADR-006 · BIF-ADR-007

decisions.title: Start with bounded routing and one retry owner
decisions.disposition: Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
decisions.body:
Area Request executionSuggested owner Gateway reliability leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Routing flexibility can increase paid attempts and change the provider processing a request. A successful fallback is useful only when the replacement remains authorized and application-compatible. The reference service needs a comprehensible baseline before adaptive strategies obscure attribution and failure analysis.

Options considered

  • Selected: explicit weighted pools, authorized fallback lists and one logical-call retry budget.
  • Rejected: retries independently enabled at client, gateway and intermediary layers.
  • Deferred: adaptive or semantic routing until a baseline demonstrates a measurable workload-specific advantage.

Proposed decision

Publish versioned aliases with bounded weighted targets and compatible fallbacks. Assign retry ownership, total deadline and attempt ceiling to the gateway service contract. Classify errors by safe retry semantics, honor upstream quota feedback where supported, and never cross residency, data-policy or retained-resource boundaries through fallback. Keep policy denials terminal, setting AllowFallbacks=false; retries must never convert denial into provider fallback.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Predictable routing simplifies diagnosis and provider-capacity planning while leaving some adaptive optimization unrealized.
  • Retries can still create billable failed attempts; application side effects need separate idempotency protection.

Required validation

  • Injected authentication, quota, timeout and server errors produce only the approved number and destination of attempts.
  • Every fallback preserves policy and reports attempt cost; exhausted deadlines terminate work coherently. Terminal policy denial produces no subsequent provider attempt.

Revisit trigger

Revisit after representative traffic establishes a baseline and a proposed strategy demonstrates better cost, quality or resilience without widening the policy envelope.
